1                                      INTRODUCTION

2    Q.   Please state your name and business address.

3    A.   My name is Edison Jimenez. My business address is the New Mexico Public

4         Regulation Commission (“Commission” or “NMPRC”), P.O. Box 1269, Santa Fe,

5         NM 87504.

6

7    Q.   What is your position with the Commission?

8    A.   I am employed as a Public Utilities Economist in the Utility Division Staff (“Staff”)

9         of the NMPRC.

10

11   Q.   Please describe your educational background and professional experience.

12   A.   I hold a Master of Science in Economics and a PhD in Economics, both degrees

13        from the Universidad Autonoma de Baja California in Tijuana, Mexico. My

14        undergraduate degree is a Bachelor of Business Administration, from the

15        Universidad del Tolima in Ibague, Colombia. Additionally, I hold an associate

16        degree in Accounting and Finance from SENA in Ibague, Colombia. I joined the

17        NMPRC’s Utility Division as a Public Utilities Economist within the Economics

18        Bureau in March 2023. During this time, I have attended several presentations,

19        seminars, trainings and workshops. In November 2024, I attended the NMPRC’s

20        seminar “Powering New Mexico: The Journey to Sustainable Energy”; in July 2024,

21        I attended the “EEI Electric Rates Course: Rates in a Changing Industry” provided

22        by the Edison Electric Institute (“EEI”); in November 2023, I attended the NMPRC’s

23        seminar “Regulation in New Mexico – How to Navigate a Dynamic Landscape”;
                                                   1
                                     CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                               PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                    EDISON JIMENEZ, PhD


1         and in May 2023, I attended “The Basics – Practical Regulatory Training for the

2         Electric Industry” provided by the Center for Public Utilities of NMSU.

3

4         Prior to my employment with the NMPRC, I was employed as a Research Assistant

5         at the Universitat de Barcelona in Spain and Universidad Autonoma de Baja

6         California in Mexico in the areas of Econometrics, Development Economics and

7         Industrial Development. Prior to this, I was employed as a Financial Advisor and

8         Project Analyst at Tamara & Asociados Consultorias Ltda in Barranquilla,

9         Colombia. I have been published in economics journals and continue to act as a

10        juror for economics scientific articles in peer reviewed journals in Spain, Mexico

11        and Colombia.

12

13   Q.   Have you previously provided testimony before the Commission?

14   A.   Yes. See Exhibit EJ-1 for a list of cases in which I have provided testimony,

15        affirmations or recommendations.

16

17   Q.   What is your responsibility in this case??

18   A.   My responsibility in this case is to provide Staff’s review and recommendations

19        regarding certain rate design aspects of Southwestern Public Service Company’s

20        Application for Authority to Change Rates and for Other Approvals and

21        Authorizations (“Application”), filed on November 20, 2025. Specifically, my

22        testimony addresses Southwestern Public Service Company’s (“SPS” or the

23        “Company”) proposed revisions to Rate No. 26 - Miscellaneous Service Charges

                                                   2
                                            CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                                      PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                           EDISON JIMENEZ, PhD


1         and the Company’s proposed Service Availability Charges or Customer Charges

2         for the residential classes – Rate No. 1 – Residential Service and Rate No. 39 –

3         Residential Heating Service.

4

5    Q.   What are Staff’s recommendations as set forth in your testimony in this

6         case?

7    A.   Staff’s overall base rate design recommendations are presented in the Direct

8         Testimony of Dr. Larry Blank. My testimony focuses on Staff’s recommended

9         Service Availability Charges for the Residential Service and Residential Heating

10        Service classes. Staff recommends approval of a $15.00 Service Availability

11        Charge for the residential classes in this case. As discussed in greater detail below,

12        Staff’s recommendation is in the public interest because it is consistent with the

13        Commission’s long-standing policy of gradualism, especially at a time when energy

14        affordability is of great concern to the Commission.1 At the same time, Staff’s

15        recommendation reasonably moves the fixed monthly Service Availability Charges

16        closer to cost of service to mitigate intra-class subsidization and to provide

17        customers with better price signals.

18

19        Additionally, my testimony provides Staff’s recommendation for approval of SPS’s

20        proposed revisions to its Miscellaneous Service Charges. As discussed in the

21        following section of my testimony, the Company’s Miscellaneous Service Charges



          1
              See Direct Testimony of Ed Rilkoff for a broader discussion about affordability.

                                                              3
                                         CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                                   PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                        EDISON JIMENEZ, PhD


1         have not been updated since September 27, 2018, pursuant to Commission Order

2         in Case No. 17-00255-UT.2 It is in the public interest for the Commission to approve

3         revised Miscellaneous Service Charges that fully and adequately recover the costs

4         of providing such services to avoid the potential for unrecovered costs to be borne

5         by all SPS’s electric service customers, rather than only those customers that

6         cause the costs to be incurred.

7

8                            MISCELLANEOUS SERVICE CHARGES

9    Q.   Did Staff raise concerns about SPS’s Rate No. 26 – Miscellaneous Service

10        Charges in SPS’s last rate case, Case 22-00286-UT?

11   A.   Yes. In that case, SPS did not present any changes to its Miscellaneous Service

12        Charges, nor did the Company provide any support or analysis demonstrating that

13        the existing charges adequately recover the costs for providing the various service

14        charges contained in Rate No. 26. SPS’s Miscellaneous Service Charges have not

15        changed in the Company’s previous three base rate cases, Case Nos. 19-00170-

16        UT, 20-00238-UT and 22-00286-UT. Given that SPS had not proposed any

17        adjustments to the charges in several years, Staff’s concern is that if the

18        Miscellaneous Service Charges do not fully and adequately recover the costs of

19        providing those services, the unrecovered costs will be borne by all SPS’s electric

20        service customers, and not just those customers that cause the costs to be

21        incurred.


          2
           See Case 17-00255-UT, In the Matter of Southwestern Public Service Company’s Application for
          Revision of its Retail Electric Rates Pursuant to Advice Notice No. 272, filed on October 27, 2017.

                                                          4
                                           CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                                     PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                          EDISON JIMENEZ, PhD


1    Q.   What was Staff’s recommendation concerning SPS’s Miscellaneous Service

2         Charges in Case No. 22-00286-UT?

3    A.   Staff recommended that SPS be required to provide full cost support for each of

4         the Company’s Miscellaneous Service Charges in its next base rate case (the

5         instant case) and propose changes to the level of charges and the miscellaneous

6         services offered as appropriate to ensure undue costs are not being borne by all

7         SPS’s electric service customers. Case No. 22-00286-UT was a stipulated case,

8         and Staff’s recommendation was not specifically addressed by the stipulation in

9         that case. However, the Company agreed to provide cost support for each of its

10        Miscellaneous Service charges in this case).3

11

12   Q.   Has the Company complied with Staff’s past recommendation in the current

13        Application?

14   A.   Yes. SPS has presented the updated Miscellaneous Service Charges in its

15        Application, which are detailed in Attachment TJH-5 to the Direct Testimony of

16        Taylor J. Hurt.

17

18   Q.   Please, briefly explain the updates made by the Company?

19   A.   The various cost components contained under Rate No. 26 – Miscellaneous

20        Service Charges have been updated to reflect the cost of providing the associated

21        services. Some of the charges have been updated to reflect actual costs such as

6   As can be observed, charges such as the After Hours Connection, Reconnect and

7   Out of Cycle Meter Reading charges have received a significant reduction. As

8   explained by SPS’s witness Hurt,4 such reductions in costs are a benefit of the

        See Direct Testimony of Taylor Hurt at pages 39-40.

                               PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF

1         remote capabilities that have been achieved with advanced metering technology.

2         On the other hand, the increases are the result of inflation adjustment for a long

3         time due, which is required to reflect the current costs. Furthermore, the Returned

4         Check Charge has been increased to reflect the actual amounts that are charged

5         to SPS by the banks with which the Company does business.

6

7    Q.   What is the revenue impact of SPS’s proposed changes to Miscellaneous

8         Service Charges?

9    A.   The overall impact is a reduction of $59,563 in SPS’s miscellaneous revenues.

10        This effect is a result of the proposed decrease in the Reconnect Charge.

11        Attachment TJH-5 (Miscellaneous Charges Workpaper) to the Direct Testimony of

12        Taylor J. Hurt reflects the average current Miscellaneous revenue of $2,806,668.75

13        in comparison to the proposed revenue of $2,747,105.73 in this Application.

14

15   Q.   Does Staff recommend approval of SPS’s proposed adjustments to its

16        Miscellaneous Service Charges?

17   A.   Yes. After reviewing the workpapers presented by SPS’s witness Hurt, Staff agrees

18        with SPS’s methodology for calculating the rates, including the adjustments for

19        inflation. As indicated above, it is reasonable and appropriate to establish these

20        rates at cost of service. The total miscellaneous revenues are reduced by $59,563

21        as a result of the Company’s proposed decrease to the Meter Reconnect Fee.

22

                                         CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                                   PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                        EDISON JIMENEZ, PhD


1                         RESIDENTIAL SERVICE AVAILABILITY CHARGES

2    Q.   What Service Availability Charge is SPS proposing for the Residential

3         Service and Residential Heating Service classes?

4    A.   SPS is proposing a fixed monthly Service Availability Charge or customer charge

5         of $21.00 for both Residential Service and Residential Heating Service. This

6         represents an increase of $9.80 (87.50%) above SPS’s current residential

7         customer charges of $11.20.

8

9    Q.   How does SPS’s proposed monthly customer charge for Residential Service

10        and Residential Heating Service customers compare to the monthly

11        customer charges of other regulated investor-owned electric utilities in New

12        Mexico?

13   A.   As shown on the Table 2, SPS’s proposed monthly customer charge of $21.00 is

14        higher than both El Paso Electric Company’s (“EPE”) Commission-approved

15        charge of $7.00, and Public Service Company of New Mexico’s (“PNM”)

16        Commission-approved charge of $11.93. However, it should be noted that EPE

17        received a rate decrease in its last rate case (20-00104-UT), and EPE’s monthly

18        customer charge did not change from its previously existing charge as a result of

19        that case. Additionally, PNM’s current customer charge of $11.93 is the result of

20        negotiations and settlement in Case No. 24-00089-UT.5 These factors may have

1    Q.   Does Staff support SPS’s proposed increase to its Service Availability

2         Charge for Residential Service and Residential Heating Service?

3    A.   Staff supports the concept behind SPS’s proposal to move toward fully recovering

4         customer component costs through the Service Availability Charge for all rates.

5         Moving customer charges closer to their cost of service reduces intra-class

6         subsidization and provides customers with better price signals. Additionally,

7         increasing the fixed monthly charge improves revenue stability and helps to

8         mitigate the monthly fixed costs that a utility incurs regardless of the usage levels

9         of its customers.

10

11        However, SPS asserts that the proposed monthly charge for both Residential

12        Service and Residential Heating Service will not recover the full customer

13        component cost of service. According to SPS witness Trowbridge, this is because

14        he has designed the Service Availability Charge to collect 75.00% of the fixed

15        customer-related costs or revenue requirement allocated to the residential class in

16        an effort to gradually increase the charge to reflect full cost causality.7

17

18        Staff has traditionally advocated for gradual increases on the fixed monthly

19        customer charges, specifically for residential customers, arguing that increases in

20        the fixed monthly charge have a greater impact on low usage customers and those

21        who have invested in energy efficiency measures, rather than on high usage



          7
              See Direct Testimony of Alexander G. Trowbridge at page 24, lines 10-18.

                                                           10
                                      CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                                PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                     EDISON JIMENEZ, PhD


1         customers. Higher fixed charges do less to promote conservation, limit customers

2         control over their bills, and have a more significant impact on residential customers

3         than increases in the fixed customer charge for a large customer that uses more

4         power.

5

6         In this case, Staff does not support SPS’s proposed $9.80 increase on the Service

7         Availability Charge for the Residential Service or the Residential Heating Service

8         classes. In Staff’s opinion, the proposed increase is not consistent with the

9         Commission’s long-standing policy of gradualism. Staff believes that an 87.50%

10        increase in the customer charge, even though, as SPS claims, it recovers only

11        75% of the customer-related costs, is excessive and could potentially result in rate

12        shock, especially for low usage customers.

13

14   Q.   What is Staff’s recommended Service Availability Charge or customer

15        charge for residential customers?

16   A.   Staff recommends a Service Availability Charges of $15.00 for the Residential

17        Service and Residential Heating Service classes, which represents an increase of

18        $3.80 or 33.93%. This more moderate increase will provide customers with better

19        price signals and will allow for a smoother transition to the new rates. Under Staff’s

20        cost of service, the Residential Customer Charge of $15.00 will allow the Company

21        to recover 57.7% of the customer-related costs in the Revenue Requirement

22        assigned to the Residential classes. Staff’s rate design calculations are presented

23        by Dr. Blank in his Direct Testimony on behalf of NMPRC Utility Division Staff.

                                                   11
                                    CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                              PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                   EDISON JIMENEZ, PhD


1

2        Staff’s proposed Residential customer charge is in line with past Staff’s positions

3        in other Rate cases and is consistent with the Commission’s long-standing policy

4        of gradualism. At the same time, Staff’s proposed customer charge continues to

5        provide reasonable movement toward fully recovering customer component costs

6        through the customer charge, which will reduce intra-class subsidies.

7

8   Q.   Does this conclude your testimony?

9   A.   Yes.
